area.title: Layout, navigation, sign-in and shared page chrome
area.scope: What every page shares: the GOV.UK header, service name, service navigation and its items, phase banner and feedback link, footer, page title pattern, section captions, back links, error summary and shared error messages, error pages, the prototype index and version cards, sign-in, organisation choice, sign-out and sessions across services, security headers, and the accessibility and security suites. Stops at the journey's step order and scope rules (journey-flow). Includes the high-risk plants frontend's shared layout, kit, save actions and shared copy, and its chrome, sign-in, accessibility and Welsh rulings.

sources.role: the decision that pagination is kept everywhere and that its earlier removal was an error: every address book list and every address picker pages, and no requirement says a list of an organisation's addresses is served or shown unpaginated. It drops req-611's 'unpaginated' clause and supersedes ruling:ian-2026-11-23 point 6 on that point alone, because that point's reasoning rested on the address book's list endpoint taking no role and so having to be read whole and paged for display, which is no longer true of the service: RequestedListFilters takes roles and searchRoles, AddressController lists one page at a time with page and pageSize, and ListPaging sets 1 to 100 defaulting to 25, exactly the bounds ruling:paul-2026-11-05 point 8 names. The role filter runs in the service before the page is cut, so paging the API cannot make it wrong, and Paul's point 8 stands in full. The rest of ruling:ian-2026-11-23 stands: the pickers page at eight, the one-page clause of inc-087's criteria 7, 8 and 9 stays dropped with req-594 and req-595, and the 'Selected address' restatement comes back with the paging. EUDPA-827 is the fix and has landed on the animals frontend's main. It settles conflict c-292 by keeping the plants contact picker's pagination and inset, and the contact picker pages at eight rather than five, confirmed by Ian the same day, so every picker in both journeys pages at the figure the INS address book list already uses and ruling:ian-2026-11-23 point 1 set for the other pickers.

sources.role: the decision that the live animals and high-risk plants party pickers page at eight, and that the one-page clause of inc-087's criteria 7, 8 and 9 is dropped along with req-594, req-595 and the paging and inset half of c-094's outcome. The clause rested on ruling-sam-2026-10-09-pm-p3-041, which that file heads as the orchestrator's application of Sam's principle rather than a ruling of Sam's: point 3b is about live filtering alone, and the bullet three lines above builds the INS address book list at 8 a page over the same records. The prototype's single page is read off a book too small to need paging, so it is evidence either way only under ruling-sam-2026-10-09-p1-116, which keeps the prototype to look and feel rather than architecture; ruling:ian-2026-11-11 point 2 is not the ground, being scoped to app/data and data claims. Eight is the INS address book list's figure alone: the transporter list renders no pagination yet, EUDPA-824 being To Do. The 'Selected address' inset comes back with the paging, because req-595's own reason for dropping it was that one page put the chosen row always on screen. req-611 is unaffected: the address book's role-scoped list stays unpaginated, because each frontend reads the whole book to filter by role and pages what is left for display.

claims.statement: The live animals and high-risk plants party pickers show eight of a role's addresses a page.
claims.quote: The pickers page at eight, and the one-page clause of `inc-087`'s criteria 7, 8 and 9 is dropped.
claims.note: New. Answers the report question the bug raised against inc-087 criterion 7.

claims.statement: The one-page clause of inc-087's acceptance criteria 7, 8 and 9 is dropped.
claims.quote: the one-page clause of `inc-087`'s criteria 7, 8 and 9 is dropped
claims.note: New. The clause this ruling withdraws, named by criterion.

claims.statement: Eight a page is the figure the INS address book list already uses, which is why the pickers take it.
claims.quote: Eight is the figure the INS address book list already uses (`insfrontend:src/server/app/features/address-book/list/list.controller.js:49`, `REQ-INS-ADDR-013`).
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The animals transporter list is not a precedent for how many addresses a page holds, because it renders no pagination today and the ticket to split it into pages of eight is still to do.
claims.quote: The animals transporter list is **not** a precedent: it renders no pagination today, and EUDPA-824, the ticket to split it into pages of eight, is still To Do.
claims.note: New. Refuses a precedent rather than setting one.

claims.statement: Paging the pickers sits on top of the role filtering, which stays as it is.
claims.quote: Paging comes back on top of the role filtering, which is correct and stays.
claims.note: New. Leaves the role filtering inc-087 built untouched.

claims.statement: The one-page clause was a distillation error: it rests on a claim that is the orchestrator's application of Sam's principle on live filtering, not a ruling of Sam's on how many addresses a page holds.
claims.quote: **It was a distillation error, and the error is identifiable.** The clause rests on `ruling-sam-2026-10-09-pm-p3-041`, which is the orchestrator's application of Sam's principle, not a ruling of Sam's on paging
claims.note: New. Names the claim the withdrawn clause rested on.

claims.statement: Sam's point 3b rules on when results refresh, not on how many addresses a page holds.
claims.quote: It rules on when results refresh, not on how many a page holds.
claims.note: New. The ground on which the earlier claim is read as not covering paging.

claims.statement: The same afternoon ruling builds the INS address book list at eight a page three lines above the sentence that removed the pickers' paging, over the same address-book records, so one page of it holds two incompatible answers, and eight is the one with a requirement behind it.
claims.quote: One ruling, one page of it, two incompatible answers to how many addresses a page holds. Eight is the one with a requirement behind it.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The prototype showing one page of addresses is a fixture of an address book too small to need paging, not a requirement that a page holds every address.
claims.quote: **The prototype's single page is a fixture, not a requirement.** `prototype-dr2-1-source-p8-063` reads one page off the prototype's own address book, which holds too few records to need paging, so the prototype could not show paging whether it wanted it or not.
claims.note: New. Sets aside the prototype claim behind the one-page clause.

claims.statement: How many rows a page holds over a real dataset that grows is not look and feel, so the prototype is not the authority for it.
claims.quote: It rests instead on `ruling-sam-2026-10-09-p1-116`, "Prototype is the authority for how things look and feel not how they are architected": how many rows a page holds over a real dataset that grows is not look and feel
claims.note: New. Says which earlier claim point 4 rests on, and which it does not.

claims.statement: The "Selected address: <name>" restatement comes back with the paging, between the search box and the results, in the words both frontends already had.
claims.quote: The inset goes back where it was, between the search box and the results, with the words both frontends already had.
claims.note: New. Reverses req-595's removal of the inset.

claims.statement: The reason req-595 gave for dropping the restatement no longer holds, because the chosen row can be on another page again and a trader on page two would otherwise have nothing on screen telling them what they have chosen.
claims.quote: Once the chosen row can be on another page again, that reason is gone: a trader on page two would otherwise have nothing on screen telling them what they have chosen.
claims.note: New. Why the inset returns rather than merely that it does.

claims.statement: The address book's own role-scoped list stays unpaginated: each frontend reads the whole book because the list endpoint takes no role, filters by role itself, and then pages what is left for display.
claims.quote: The address book's own role-scoped list stays unpaginated: each frontend reads the whole book because the list endpoint takes no role, filters by role itself, and then pages what is left for display. Paging the API would make the role filter wrong.
claims.note: New. Leaves req-611 as it is.

claims.statement: inc-087 stays done, because it was built as its criteria then read, and the code, the criteria, the requirements behind them, c-094's outcome and the behaviour spec are corrected under EUDPA-827 so a re-distillation does not drop paging or the restatement again.
claims.quote: **`inc-087` stays done.** It was built as its criteria then read. The code is corrected under EUDPA-827, which also corrects the criteria, the requirements behind them, `c-094`'s outcome and the behaviour spec, so a re-distillation does not drop paging or the restatement again.
claims.note: New. Says the increment is not reopened and where the correction lands.

claims.statement: The ruling does not say what the pickers offer once a search narrows a role's list to eight or fewer, so whether pagination disappears on a narrowed list is left open here.
claims.note: New. The ruling fixes the page size and the restatement but says nothing about a search narrowing the list below the threshold; the behaviour spec settles it.

sources.role: the owner's answers to the overview and review theme's engineering review: plants shows the notification task list heading visibly as live animals does, reading "Notification task list" in both services; each posting button on the notification view header gets its own form, as every other posting button in the service does, so Amend and Copy as new each post their own and Delete stays a link to the delete confirmation page outside both, in the live animals and plants frontends; tests find live animals review cards by GOV.UK structure and role rather than by the words of a numbered heading; every other atypical item the review found is fixed, except the local stack's automatic uploader restart, the plants journey spec ruling deleted rather than superseded, the tests repo's deleted docs note on why Cancel amend waits on the URL, and the animals backend unit tests that build a real DocumentService on stubbed repositories; and the fixes land in as few increments as sensible rather than one per item. It also replaces the 16 November ruling's "what stays" clause on outstanding items: the animals backend stops storing the outstanding items list and the rule that works it out comes off the OutstandingItem enum, both re-added with the future outstanding-actions banner, while the submitted date is still recorded. "Answers differ from submitted" is a non-null yes or no flag, which the animals frontend's local stub takes from the backend's shape rather than working out itself.

sources.role: the decision that the exporter clause of inc-087 acceptance criterion 2 is dropped and no EXPORTER role is to be added anywhere. The clause rested on two prototype claims reading the prototype internal consignor-or-exporter type vocabulary (app/routes.js, app/data/consignment-address-sections.js) as a domain role, which ruling:ian-2026-11-11 point 2 already bars and which ruling:sam-2026-10-09 claim 22 gives to the address book service as architecture rather than look and feel. What the prototype means is that one section covers both parties under the heading Consignor, which the real service already models as the single CONSIGNOR role and inc-087 already satisfies. The bar on app/data is on what the file is, not on how a claim is labelled: a rule claim from those files is refused as readily as a data one.

claims.statement: The ruling leaves open what happens to the templates work: it calls templates concept work but does not say whether templates are parked, deferred, dropped or still built for the deadline, and names no increment or requirement for them.
The ruling leaves open who picks the parked address-search work back up, when, and what would unpark it: it says only that it is not needed yet.

The country search on the live animals, germinal products and high-risk plants origin pages is the GOV.UK accessible autocomplete the real service's main branch already uses, not the prototype's hand-built search: decided item 1 says the country search 'keeps' that component's own announcements, which only holds if the component itself stays, so nothing is built to replace it.
claims.ref: ruling-sam-2026-11-09.md claim 1, read with the context paragraph (line 15)
claims.quote: **The country search keeps the accessible autocomplete's own announcements.**
claims.note: The extract records what is not announced (claims ruling-sam-2026-11-09-p1-008 and -009) and that the component's own announcements stand (-007), but no claim records the component decision itself: main's accessible autocomplete stays and the prototype's hand-built search is not carried over. This is the decision that makes the dropped criteria safe to drop, so reconcile needs it when it judges whether anything is left to build on the origin pages.

sources.role: the decision on what the address book stores for an address's type and uses (EUDPA-711): "use" is renamed "role" everywhere, in the record, the API, the code, the copy keys, the tests and the spec, and an address holds the roles it can play on a notification, being place of origin, consignor, consignee, importer, place of destination and branch address. The address book stores roles only and requires at least one; it does not store an address type and ignores one a client sends, the address type being the INS front door's grouping of roles worked out from them. The grouping of roles into sending, receiving and branch is the address book's internal rule rather than part of its API, and it refuses roles from more than one group, and a consignee, importer or place of destination outside the United Kingdom. The list takes role, repeatable and any-of, and searchRole, in place of addressType, use and searchUse. A role a new notification type needs is added in code, each role in exactly one group. Addresses saved before the change are not migrated: after release the addresses collection is dropped in dev and test with CDP tooling and the address book restarted, and locally the stack is restarted. The address book's list and every address picker keep pagination even though the Design Release 2.1 prototype has none, the list API paging with page and pageSize of 1 to 100 defaulting to 25, because organisations in test environments hold thousands of addresses; no requirement to list an organisation's addresses unpaginated is built, which ruling:ian-2026-11-23 point 6 later reads the other way for req-611 and so outranks on that point alone.

sources.role: the owner's decisions: outranks every other source. Search boxes use the real frontend's accessible component with MDM's entries. JavaScript behaviour follows the toolbox rule with graceful degradation; JavaScript-only prototype behaviour, pop-ups included, waits on design in its own theme. Commodity catalogue and search wait on MDM; transporter management waits on requirements; the INS dashboard's summary information waits on its requirements. The overview, review, declaration and confirmation are set-owned, and shared parts change add-only. Where plants has the same page or behaviour, the same increment changes it. Each notification list is reframed in its own frontend. The report groups work as ready or blocked. Claims marked as the orchestrator's apply Sam's principles and are not his rulings; ruling:sam-2026-10-09-templates covers templates and the dashboard narrowing.

sources.role: the owner's decisions, as narrowed by ruling:sam-2026-10-09: on look and feel the prototype wins by default over what the real services do today; only a DR1 judgement on the same difference, or a real constraint the prototype cannot express (persistence, validation, authentication, cross-service behaviour), overrides it. The prototype never decides architecture.

claims.quote: The DR1 parity backlog. [...] It is not a source of requirements.

claims.statement: Nothing is built because the DR1 parity backlog says so on its own; this follows from the backlog not being a source of requirements and being usable only where the real frontend and the prototype clash.

claims.quote: It is not a source of requirements. Use it only when the real frontend and the prototype clash
claims.note: New. The main session's claim 3 states this in so many words; the quote implies it.

claims.statement: The DR1 parity backlog is used only where the real frontend and the prototype clash.
claims.quote: Use it only when the real frontend and the prototype clash
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Where DR1 already made a judgement on that same difference between the real frontend and the prototype, the DR1 judgement is followed.
claims.quote: if DR1 already made a judgement on that difference, follow it and cite the row.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Where a DR1 judgement is followed, the DR1 parity backlog row it comes from is cited.
claims.quote: follow it and cite the row.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The prototype (Design Release 2.1) wins by default over what the real services do today.
claims.quote: Precedence: the prototype wins by default.
claims.note: New. 'Over what the real services do today' is the main session's framing; it follows from the Goal paragraph.

claims.statement: A DR1 judgement on the same difference overrides the prototype default.
claims.quote: Only a DR1 judgement or a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. 'On the same difference' comes from the DR1 paragraph (lines 8-9).

claims.statement: A real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default; the ruling names persistence, validation, authentication and cross-service behaviour as such constraints.
claims.quote: a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. The quote says 'auth'; claim 6 reads it as authentication. Claim 6 adds 'such as', making the list examples; the quote's parenthesis can be read either as examples or as the full list.

claims.statement: Nothing other than a DR1 judgement on the same difference or a real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype.
claims.quote: Only a DR1 judgement or a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. In particular, what a real service does today is not on its own a reason to depart from the prototype.

claims.statement: Questions for people are kept to a minimum.
claims.quote: Decisions: keep questions for people to a minimum.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: A question for people is raised only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the prototype default nor a DR1 judgement settles it.
claims.quote: Raise one only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the default nor DR1 settles it.
claims.note: New. Both conditions must hold. 'The default' is read as the prototype-wins default from the Precedence paragraph.

claims.statement: Increments are grouped into themes, and the themes are drawn from the evidence.
claims.quote: Themes: group the increments into themes based on the evidence.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Each theme's boundary is set by the code it touches.
claims.quote: Draw the boundaries by the code each one touches
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Themes can be built in parallel on separate machines without pull requests that conflict with each other.
claims.quote: so themes can be built in parallel on separate machines without conflicting PRs.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The ruling's DR1 paragraph has an elision marked [...]: what the omitted words said about the DR1 parity backlog is not recorded.
The ruling does not say what makes a difference 'truly exceptional', so when a question for people is warranted is left open.

The ruling limits DR1 use to clashes between 'the real frontend' and the prototype; it does not say which frontend that is, or whether DR1 judgements apply to differences in the INS frontend, the backends or other repos.
The ruling does not say which override wins when a DR1 judgement and a real constraint the prototype cannot express point different ways on the same difference.
The ruling does not say what a real service does where a real constraint overrides the prototype: whether it keeps today's behaviour or matches the prototype as closely as the constraint allows.
The ruling does not say whether a feature or behaviour a real service has that Design Release 2.1 does not show at all counts as a difference to remove, or is left alone.
The ruling does not say what to do where the code two themes need to touch overlaps, so no boundary keeps their pull requests from conflicting.

sources.role: DR1 judgements only. Never a source of requirements on its own. Used only where the real frontend and the prototype clash: where DR1 already judged that same difference, the judgement wins and its row is cited.

claims.statement: Where the trader picks several things across several searches, the page offers a search box whose results they tick; without JavaScript the Search button posts the page and the server renders the results again, and with JavaScript the results refresh in place with nothing reloading.

Without JavaScript it is a submitted
search: the Search button posts the page's form with `action=search`, and the
server renders the page again with the results. With JavaScript the results
refresh in place as the trader types, ticks, removes or clears, and nothing
reloads.

Because the page renders the results on both paths, the matching, the order,
the labels, the bold text and the validation each have one owner, on the

claims.statement: Refreshes of a multi-select search run one at a time, each posted only once the one before it has landed, so two never reach the server at once and a search pressed straight after Clear all does not post the cleared choices again.

Refreshes run one at a time. Each is posted only once the one before it has
  landed, from the form that one left

claims.statement: Saving straight after a tick, a Remove or Clear all saves what the trader can see: a button outside the search waits for any refresh still in flight, and a typed search still waiting on the pause is dropped.

If refreshes are still on their way, the submit waits for them to land,
  so a save pressed straight after Clear all or a Remove saves what the trader
  sees. A typed search still waiting for the trader to pause is dropped.

claims.statement: After the results refresh, the keyboard stays where it was: focus returns to the same control, moves to the search box when that control has gone, and is left alone when the trader has moved it elsewhere.

After a swap, focus goes back to the element with the same id. If that element
  has gone, such as a Remove button, focus moves to the search box. If the
  trader has moved focus elsewhere while the results refreshed, it stays there.

claims.statement: If a refresh of the results fails or cannot reach the server, the page posts itself instead, so the trader carries on with the version that needs no JavaScript.

claims.statement: The exclusion is held to be an upstream disagreement between govuk-frontend's conditional-reveal radios, which set aria-expanded on the radio input, and axe's aria-allowed-attr rule, and not a defect in the service.

claims.statement: The security scan is dynamic application security testing with OWASP ZAP as a proxy: Playwright drives real signed-in journeys through it instead of letting ZAP crawl, so ZAP attacks what a real session touched.
claims.quote: A DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scan using [OWASP ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/) as a proxy. Playwright drives real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl, so it observes what a real session touches and then attacks that.

claims.statement: Scan coverage is traffic-driven, so any route no spec drives is invisible to the scan; the attacking corpus is therefore curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.quote: Coverage is therefore **traffic-driven**: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan. That is why the `@active` corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.note: Stated in general terms: the weakness is one of coverage, not of any particular route.

claims.statement: There are two security profiles: a passive one that runs the end-to-end suite without the attacking specs and does not attack, and an attacking one that runs only the attacking specs and is deliberate and docker-compose only.
claims.quote:
| `security`        | The e2e suite, excluding `@active` | No — passive only | Cheap, run broadly              |
| `security:active` | The `@active` suite only           | Yes               | Deliberate; docker-compose only |

claims.statement: The attacking specs are kept out of the passive profile because they walk the same journeys a second time and include destructive steps.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, note under the Profiles table
claims.quote: `@active` is excluded from the passive profile because it walks the same journeys a second time and includes destructive steps.

claims.statement: The attacking profile is refused on the CDP platform: the attacking specs delete notifications, documents and dead-letter messages and the scan refires each with fuzzed payloads, which is acceptable against a throwaway stack and destructive against a shared one, so the entrypoint fails the run instead.
claims.quote: The `@active` suite deletes notifications, documents and DLQ messages, and the active scan re-fires each with fuzzed payloads — fine against a disposable stack, destructive against a shared one. `entrypoint.sh` writes to `FAILED` rather than running it.

claims.statement: Guarding only the production environment is not enough to keep the attacking profile off shared environments, because such a guard would still have let dev, test and perf-test run it.
claims.quote: The `throwIfProdEnvironment` guard is no help here: it stops `prod` alone, so `dev`, `test` and `perf-test` would all have run.

claims.statement: The scan runs in three lanes that do not share a configuration or a target: locally against the localhost stack in either profile, from a GitHub Action against a stack on the runner in the attacking profile, and on the CDP portal against a deployed environment in the passive profile only.
claims.quote: | **CDP portal**    | `PROFILE` env var → `entrypoint.sh`                                                                         | `playwright.config.ts`                | deployed `${ENVIRONMENT}` | `security` or `<domain>:security` only  |

claims.statement: The GitHub Action that runs the attacking scan is manual dispatch only and its nightly schedule stays switched off until an end-to-end run has been verified.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, paragraph after the lanes table
claims.quote: The GitHub Action is manual dispatch only; the nightly schedule stays disabled pending a verified end-to-end run.

claims.statement: The attacking scan's report is published to a public GitHub Pages site under a dated path and is password-protected for that reason, and reports older than seven days are deleted.
claims.quote: Its report publishes to GitHub Pages under `security-active/<date>/`, password-protected via the `ZAP_REPORT_PASSWORD` secret because that Pages site is otherwise public. Reports older than 7 days are pruned.
claims.note: The password itself is a repository secret and is not in the source; nothing here names a value.

claims.statement: Six services are in the scan, each as its own named ZAP context: the animals frontend, the animals admin, the INS frontend, the animals backend, the plants backend and the address book.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'What gets scanned' table, and zap/automation-context.yaml env.contexts
claims.quote:
| `trade-imports-animals-frontend` | 3000       | `frontend`        |
| `trade-imports-animals-admin`    | 3001       | `admin`           |
| `trade-imports-ins-frontend`     | 3002       | `ins`             |
| `trade-imports-animals-backend`  | 8085       | `animals-backend` |
| `trade-imports-plants-backend`   | 8091       | `plants-backend`  |
| `trade-imports-address-book`     | 8089       | `address-book`    |

claims.statement: Each context's address is supplied by its own environment variable rather than hard-coded, so the same plans point at the compose stack's ports locally and at a per-service subdomain on CDP.
claims.ref: zap/automation-context.yaml env.contexts urls; docs/security.md, 'Ports are the compose stack's'
claims.quote: Ports are the compose stack's; on CDP each service is a per-service subdomain.

claims.statement: Diagnostic endpoints are left out of every context rather than scanned: health and static assets on the three Node apps, and health, info, metrics, cache and env on the three Java services.
claims.ref: docs/security.md, 'Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned'; zap/automation-context.yaml excludePaths for every context
claims.quote: Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned: `/health` and static assets on the Node contexts, and the full actuator set (`/health`, `/info`, `/metrics`, `/cache`, `/env`) on the three Java services.
claims.note: The Java services' diagnostic endpoints sit on the API's own root namespace, not under a prefix, because the actuator base path is "/" in each service's own configuration.

claims.statement: The identifiers in a page or API address are declared to ZAP as data rather than structure, so each run's notification does not appear as a brand-new branch of the site tree and the identifier itself becomes something the scan can attack: the notification id and upload id on the animals frontend, the address id on the INS frontend, the reference number and upload id on the animals backend, the reference number on the plants backend, and the organisation id and address id on the address book.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml env.contexts structure.dataDrivenNodes (every context), with the frontend comment at lines 15-21
claims.quote:
dataDrivenNodes tells ZAP the segment
    # is data, not structure: one folded node, and the id becomes an
    # injection point (IDOR-style access-by-id checks included).
claims.note: This is how the suite tests for access to another organisation's record by guessing its identifier.

claims.statement: Those structure rules only apply to parts of the site tree as they are first seen, so the contexts are registered on ZAP by a plan of their own before any journey runs; registering them with the scanning plan afterwards would be too late for the identifiers to be recognised as data.
claims.quote:
Structural Modifiers (dataDrivenNodes) and excludePaths only apply to
# site-tree nodes as they're *added* — they don't retroactively reshape
# nodes that already exist.

claims.statement: The context-registration plan declares one do-nothing job only because a plan must have at least one, there being no traffic yet to wait for.
claims.quote:
# No traffic exists yet at this point in the run, so there's nothing to
  # wait for — this job only exists because a plan needs at least one job.

claims.statement: All three ZAP plans must declare exactly the same contexts, and a run stops with an explanatory error before registering anything if they have drifted apart, because ZAP offers no way to share that block between plans.
claims.quote: `env.contexts in ${mismatches.join(', ')} doesn't match ${BASELINE_FILE} — ZAP has no way to share this block across plans, so all three must be kept identical.`

claims.statement: The attacking plan runs one attack job per context, six in all, each capped at 60 minutes.
claims.quote:
- type: activeScan
    parameters:
      context: frontend
      ... 
      maxScanDurationInMins: 60
claims.note: Quote abbreviated across the job's comment block; the same two parameters appear on each of the six jobs.

claims.statement: The 60-minute cap is a runaway guard rather than a budget, set at about four and a half times the slowest context measured: the animals frontend took 13 minutes 27 seconds, the admin 4 minutes 39, the INS frontend 1 minute 25, the backend 1 minute 17 and the address book 21 seconds, 21 minutes in all.
claims.quote:
A runaway guard, not a budget. Measured: frontend 13m27s, admin 4m39s,
      # ins 1m25s, backend 1m17s, address-book 21s — 21m total, frontend 64% of
      # it. 60 is ~4.5x the slowest, leaving room for CI (2 vCPU, ~2-3x local)
      # and for the corpus to roughly double.

claims.statement: The cap in the plan and the figure the gate checks against must be changed together and must match exactly, or a cut-short scan would pass unnoticed.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml, frontend activeScan comment; utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, ACTIVE_SCAN_CAP_MINS
claims.quote:
Change this, the six below, and ACTIVE_SCAN_CAP_MINS in
      # utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts together — they must match exactly.

claims.statement: A run fails when an attack job finished at or within half a minute of its cap, because a scan cut off part-way reporting no findings is a false clean; the fix is to raise the cap, not to overlook it.
A run fails when a declared context recorded no traffic at all, the one failure that looks like success, since nothing reached means no site-tree entry, no alerts and a clean-looking report section.
claims.quote:
Fails the run when a declared context recorded no traffic — the one failure
 * mode that looks like success, since no requests means no site-tree node, no
 * alerts, and a clean-looking report section.
claims.note: The check reads the plan rather than the report, because a context with no traffic is missing from the report entirely. It catches a context nothing drives, a spec dropped from the corpus, and the case where the API clients stop sending through the proxy.

claims.statement: The no-traffic check only runs in the attacking profile.
claims.quote: const contextsWithNoTraffic = zapProfile === 'active' ? await findContextsWithNoTraffic(client, scope?.contexts) : [];

claims.statement: An attacking run can be narrowed to one domain, and then only that domain's contexts are checked for traffic and the report is marked as a scoped run so a green scoped report is never mistaken for a full one: animals covers the animals frontend and backend, animals-admin the admin, ins the INS frontend and address book, and plants the plants backend.
claims.ref: config/zap.ts, ZAP_SCOPE_CONTEXTS and resolveZapScope; utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, scopedSection

claims.statement: An unknown domain name for a scoped run is refused with a message listing the domains that exist, rather than silently scanning everything.
claims.quote: throw new Error(`Unknown ZAP_SCOPE '${domain}'. Expected one of: ${Object.keys(ZAP_SCOPE_CONTEXTS).join(', ')}`);

claims.statement: Anything other than the exact attacking profile name is treated as passive, so a mistyped profile cannot start an attack.
Each ZAP alert type is rated from a rules file that maps ZAP's plugin ids to ignore, warn or fail, and an unlisted alert fails the build if it is high risk and only warns otherwise.
claims.quote:
Unlisted rules default to: FAIL if High risk, WARN otherwise — see
# run-and-gate.ts.
claims.note: High is chosen as the bar because it is the least noisy risk tier and so the safest starting point for a new gate; individual medium findings are to be escalated in the rules file as they are triaged.

claims.statement: An ignored alert stays visible in the report exactly as a warned one does and the difference is documentation only: it records that someone has already looked at it and judged it a known false positive.
claims.quote:
IGNORE: triaged as a known false positive — stays visible in the report
#   (same as WARN) and does not fail the build; the difference from WARN is
#   documentation only, marking that someone has already looked at it

claims.statement: No alert is suppressed or ignored today: the rules file holds its format, its defaults and two commented-out examples, and not one live rule line.
claims.ref: zap/rules.tsv, whole file (every line begins with #)
claims.quote:
# Examples:
# 10015	WARN	(Incomplete or No Cache-control and Pragma HTTP Header Set — flagged 2026-08-19, not yet triaged)
# 10096	IGNORE	(Timestamp Disclosure - Unix — triaged 2026-08-19, false positive: matches the numeric suffix of a notification reference number, not an actual timestamp)
claims.note: The two examples name findings previously seen on this suite, but as examples only: with no live line, every alert today is rated by the default rule.

claims.statement: The gate counts a failing finding once per alert type rather than once per occurrence, so a finding seen on eighty-one pages is one thing to fix.
claims.quote:
Gated per alert type, not per instance — an 81-instance finding that
    // fails the gate is one thing to fix, not 81.

claims.statement: A finding recorded twice because ZAP split one host into two entries of its site tree is counted once, while the same finding on two genuinely different hosts still counts twice.
claims.note: mechanism: groups the report's site entries by name and keeps one alert per plugin id in each group.

claims.statement: Alongside its alerts each site in the report shows how many requests reached it, as reassurance that a site with few or no findings was really reached through the proxy rather than quietly skipped.
claims.ref: utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, getMessageCount comment and the index page's Sites table

claims.statement: Each run writes a landing page with a row per site showing pass or fail, requests seen and the count of high, medium, low and informational alerts, plus a totals row, and links to the full human-readable report, the machine-readable one, the Playwright run's own report and ZAP's log.
claims.quote: Sites
claims.note: mechanism: builds the HTML landing page the CDP report viewer links to, from the report JSON and live request counts.

claims.statement: The landing page is written before the run is failed, so the report exists on disk exactly when someone needs it most.
claims.quote:
Written before the throw below, not after — a failing run is exactly
  // when someone most needs the report

claims.statement: The landing page carries a prominent notice in three cases: a scan that hit its cap, a run whose traffic-generating specs did not all pass, and a run narrowed to one domain, the first two as failures and the third as a warning.
claims.quote: The traffic-generation specs did not all succeed (outcome: ${specsOutcome}) — the findings below reflect whatever traffic ran before that, not full corpus coverage.

claims.statement: ZAP's own log and its machine-readable report are republished as plain HTML pages, because the CDP report viewer refuses anything that is not HTML and the GitHub Action's password gate only wraps HTML files.
claims.ref: utils/zap/run-and-gate.ts, ZAP_LOG_ARTEFACT and JSON_REPORT_ARTEFACT comment with wrapAsHtml

claims.statement: Both scanning plans produce one combined report, machine-readable and human-readable, covering every site ZAP touched in the session, with no filter by site.
claims.ref: zap/automation-passive.yaml and zap/automation-active.yaml, the two report jobs
claims.quote: # No sites: filter — covers every site ZAP touched this session.
claims.note: Both plans title the report 'trade-imports-animals — security scan' even though it covers six services.

claims.statement: The plans wait for passive scanning and then pause five seconds before attacking or reporting, because ZAP registers the last site a moment after the last journey finishes navigating and would otherwise reject it as an invalid site.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml and zap/automation-passive.yaml, passiveScan-wait and delay jobs
claims.quote:
ZAP's site-tree bookkeeping lags slightly behind the last spec to finish
  # navigating — without this, the activeScan jobs below can start before
  # the last site is registered ("invalid site" from ZAP).

claims.statement: The DOM-based cross-site-scripting rule is switched off on every attack job, because it needs a real browser the plain ZAP image does not ship, is far slower than the other rules, and is a poor fit for server-rendered GOV.UK Design System pages that keep client-side DOM handling to a minimum; the reflected and stored cross-site-scripting rules still run.
claims.ref: zap/automation-active.yaml, the policyDefinition on each of the six activeScan jobs
claims.quote:
Reflected/
    # stored XSS rules are unaffected and still run. Also a poor fit for
    # this app regardless: GOV.UK Design System + Nunjucks server-rendered
    # pages, GDS progressive enhancement keeps client-side DOM handling to a
    # minimum, so DOM-based XSS is a small slice of the real risk surface.

claims.statement: The passive plan carries no attack job at all and is safe to run against a real deployed environment on demand.
claims.quote:
ZAP Automation Framework plan — passive scan only, no activeScan jobs.
# Safe to run against a real deployed environment on demand, no destructive
# risk.

claims.statement: Deciding pass or fail is deliberately kept out of the ZAP plans and done afterwards by the suite's own gate, so the plans only scan and report.
claims.quote:
Gating is deliberately not done here; see
# run-and-gate.ts and rules.tsv.

claims.statement: The scan is run against the already-running ZAP rather than a fresh one, so it sees what passive scanning captured while the journeys ran.

A plan that reports an error of its own fails the run, and a plan that has not finished within five hours is abandoned with an error, that ceiling being a safety net over the worst case rather than a coverage limit.
claims.quote: throw new Error(`ZAP automation plan finished with errors: ${progress.error.join('; ')}`);

claims.statement: The suite talks to ZAP on a loopback address through a connection that ignores any proxy settings in the environment, so the platform's own outbound proxy cannot redirect those control calls.
claims.quote:
Dedicated agent with no proxyEnv so CDP's HTTP_PROXY / --use-env-proxy
// cannot redirect these loopback API calls.

claims.statement: ZAP listens on a port kept deliberately outside the workspace's two growing port ranges, because the next free slot after either range is eventually taken by the next new service.
The suite's ZAP credential and port both fall back to built-in local development values when nothing is set, so no one has to configure them day to day.
claims.quote: export const zapApiKey = process.env.ZAP_API_KEY || '[REDACTED]';
claims.note: The default value is redacted here on principle; it is a local development placeholder, not a real credential. Stated in general terms: a built-in default exists, and the environment variable overrides it.

claims.statement: A scan that finishes exactly at the time ceiling is treated as cut short, because an incomplete scan reporting nothing is a false clean.
claims.quote: A scan that finishes at the ceiling was cut short, and an incomplete scan reporting no findings is a false clean.

claims.statement: The proxy listens on a configurable port, 9095 by default, deliberately outside the workspace's two growing port ranges, and its API key is taken from the environment with a local development placeholder.
claims.quote: export const zapPort = process.env.ZAP_PORT || '9095';
claims.note: The default API key in config/zap.ts is a local development placeholder; its value is [REDACTED] here.

claims.statement: The scan treats anything other than an exact request for the attacking profile as passive, so it fails safe.
A per-domain attacking run narrows the no-traffic gate to that domain's own declared areas and the report says the run was scoped; the full run leaves every declared area gated.
claims.quote: Full `security:active` is the authoritative clean bill of health. Per-domain active sets `ZAP_SCOPE` so the no-traffic gate only covers that domain's contexts; the report callout marks the run as scoped.

claims.statement: A run with an unrecognised domain scope is refused outright, naming the domains it accepts.
claims.quote: throw new Error(`Unknown ZAP_SCOPE '${domain}'. Expected one of: ${Object.keys(ZAP_SCOPE_CONTEXTS).join(', ')}`);

claims.statement: The scheduled attacking run is manual only: the nightly schedule stays switched off until an end-to-end run has been verified, and its report is published behind a password because the site it goes to is otherwise public, with reports older than seven days pruned.
claims.quote: The GitHub Action is manual dispatch only; the nightly schedule stays disabled pending a verified end-to-end run.

claims.statement: No transporter route is driven through the security proxy, so the transporter type question, both transporter forms and a transporter's own page fall outside the scan's traffic-driven coverage.

claims.statement: From a workspace clone the docker-compose run stops before the first test unless that clone owns the stack, naming the owning clone and offering GitHub Actions instead; ALLOW_FOREIGN_STACK=1 runs anyway, and a checkout outside a workspace, such as the tests image, is never stopped.

owns the stack (`tim docker owner` in the workspace prints the owner). From
another clone it stops before the first test with "The stack belongs to
`<clone>`. Run E2E there, or push and let GitHub Actions run it." Set
`ALLOW_FOREIGN_STACK=1` to run anyway. A checkout outside a workspace, such as
the tests image, is never stopped.

claims.statement: The animals journey accessibility scans leave out govuk-frontend's two conditional-reveal radio groups, because govuk-frontend sets aria-expanded on each radio that opens a reveal and axe's aria-allowed-attr rule rejects it — a disagreement between govuk-frontend and axe rather than a service defect.

(`govukConditionalRevealRadioOnOrigin` and
`govukConditionalRevealRadiosOnReason` in `fixtures/a11y.ts`). govuk-frontend sets `aria-expanded` on

`aria-allowed-attr` rule rejects it. That is a disagreement between
govuk-frontend and axe, not a service defect.

claims.statement: A CDP run gives each test 60 seconds and each expectation 15 seconds, while a docker-compose run keeps Playwright's 30-second and 5-second defaults, because each CDP page load is a real network hop.
claims.quote:
The CDP config sets a 60s test timeout and a 15s expect timeout, against
Playwright's 30s and 5s defaults that the docker-compose config keeps. Each CDP
page load is a real network hop, so CDP needs a longer budget than the local
stack.

claims.statement: A leaked address book on the dev environment, grown to 4,882 records, made every contact-address page load fan out dozens of concurrent reads through the CDP SSL sidecar, which returned 502 and 504 responses for minutes at a time; session reuse, a per-test address-book teardown and a one-off purge removed the leak, and three clean runs then kept every test under three-quarters of its budget, so the CDP test timeout came down from 90 to 60 seconds.
claims.quote:
The suite once also timed out in bursts: a
leaked address book on dev (grown to 4,882 records) made every
`contact-address` page load fan out dozens of concurrent reads through the
CDP SSL sidecar, which returned 502/504s for a few minutes at a time. Session
reuse, a per-test address-book teardown and a one-off purge removed the leak
and the outage; three clean CDP runs then kept every test under
three-quarters of its new budget (45s, or 135s for tests marked
`test.slow()`), so the timeout came down from 90s to 60s.

claims.statement: The fifteen-document limits test sets its own 120-second timeout, because its real uploads and virus scans take 57 to 60 seconds on the local stack and about 67 seconds on CDP.
claims.quote:
`documents-limits`' fifteen-document test sets its own 120s timeout: its real
uploads and virus scans take 57–60s on the local stack and about 67s on CDP,
which left too thin a margin under the 90s a slow test gets on compose.
Re-check it if the base timeouts change.

claims.statement: Each flow step waits up to 30 seconds for its page's heading rather than for the test timeout, so a transient 502 fails the step that hit it and names the page it was waiting for.
claims.quote:
The flow helpers wait for each page's heading with `pageLoadWait`
(`config/timeouts.ts`, 30s) rather than the test timeout, so a transient 502
fails the step that hit it within 30s and names the page it was waiting for.

every address and transporter created through them once the test ends, pass or
fail, retries included.

A record a test saves through the UI is not created
through them: call `addressBookApi.trackTransporterNamed(name)` after saving a
transporter so it is deleted too. A delete that fails is logged with the
record's id and never fails the test. Records saved through the UI in any other
way, such as an address added on the add-address page or through the
handshake, are not deleted.

creates them again. `globalSetup` seeds them through its own client, so no
test's clean-up deletes them.

claims.statement: CDP blocks direct calls to its back-end services from outside its network, so a laptop run sets CDP_LOCAL=true, which sends those calls through the protected ephemeral gateway and needs a developer API key sent as x-api-key; the run stops at once if the key is missing, and a CDP Portal run needs neither setting.
claims.quote:
CDP blocks direct calls to its backend services from outside its network, so
global set-up cannot reach the backend or the address book without
`CDP_LOCAL=true`. That setting sends those calls through the protected
ephemeral gateway, which needs `DEVELOPER_API_KEY` as `x-api-key`. The run
stops at once if `CDP_LOCAL=true` and the key is missing. The CDP Portal run
sits inside CDP and needs neither.

`@ins-backend`, is a different kind: it names a service whose pull request

claims.statement: The suite recognises eight service tags, each belonging to the domains that already run it by path: @address-book, @ins-backend and @ins-frontend to ins; @animals-admin to animals-admin; @animals-backend to animals and animals-admin; @animals-frontend to animals; and @plants-backend and @plants-frontend to plants.

`@a11y`, one under `security/` must carry `@active`, and one under `e2e/` neither.

claims.statement: Linting fails a spec that carries the service tag of a service whose pull request already runs the spec's own domain by path.
claims.quote: `npm run lint` fails if a spec carries the tag of a service whose pull request already runs the spec's domain by path, as `config/service-tags.ts` maps it.

claims.statement: The tag check asks Playwright to list the tests so it reads the tags a test really has, title, describe and test tags merged, and needs no stack, sign-in or browser.
claims.quote:
Asks Playwright to list the tests, so it sees the tags a test really has

The reason the tag rules are enforced is that a spec under security/ without @active would run in every end-to-end and pull-request check, and one under a11y/ without @a11y would run in end-to-end and be missed by the accessibility run.
claims.quote:
Test types are selected by tag, not by directory: `npm test` runs a domain's
 * whole directory minus `@a11y`, `@active`, `@compose` and `@dynamics`. So a
 * spec under security/ without `@active` would run in every e2e and PR check,
 * and one under a11y/ without `@a11y` would run in e2e and be missed by the
 * a11y run.

claims.statement: @duplicated-in-frontend marks an end-to-end spec whose behaviour the frontend's own FIT suite also proves, so a reader knows the check exists in both places.
claims.quote: `@duplicated-in-frontend` marks an end-to-end spec whose behaviour the frontend's own FIT suite also proves, so a reader knows the check exists in both places.

claims.statement: The suite does not wipe the database before it runs and does not need to, because every spec creates the state it asserts on through the back-end API, scoped to that run, so the specs pass against a database holding earlier runs' records.
claims.quote:
The suite does not wipe the database before it runs, and does not need to.
Every spec creates the state it asserts on through the front door (the
backend API), scoped to that run, so the specs pass against a database that
already holds the records of earlier runs.

claims.statement: A spec asserts which journey page is open through the page object's expected URL pattern, which matches the page whichever trail its address carries, and asserts an exact trail through the on-trail pattern or exact URL built from the page objects' own slugs; a spec never types a from query itself.
claims.quote:
- Which page is open: the page object's `expectedUrlPattern(reference)`. It matches the page whichever trail its address carries.
- The exact trail: the page object's `expectedUrlPatternOnTrail(reference, places)` for a `toHaveURL` matcher, or `expectedUrlOnTrail(reference, places)` for an exact `href` value. Pass the page objects' own `slug`s and the `TRAIL_START` places. A spec never types a `?from=` query.

claims.statement: An assertion two specs share lives in a shared checks module, and a flow or page object holds no assertion.
claims.quote: - An assertion two specs share lives in a `*-checks.ts` module under `page-objects/shared/` (`journey-checks.ts`, `type-ahead-checks.ts`). A flow or page object holds no assertion.

claims.statement: Visual regression tests guard rendered composition — layout, spacing, colour and typography as the user sees the page — by comparing screenshots against committed baseline images and failing if any pixels differ outside the masked regions.
claims.quote: Visual regression tests (tagged `@visual`) guard rendered composition — layout, spacing, colour, and typography as the user sees the page. They compare screenshots against committed baseline images and fail if any pixels differ outside the masked regions.

claims.statement: Baselines are committed beside their spec files, and each platform needs its own baseline, both of which are updated when a visual change is intentional.
claims.quote: Baselines are stored alongside their spec files in `*-snapshots/` directories and must be committed. Each platform requires its own baseline — update both when visual changes are intentional.

claims.statement: Visual specs run headless whatever the project setting, because headed mode uses the operating system's font rendering, which produces pixel differences against a headless baseline.
claims.quote: Visual specs run headless whatever the project setting, because headed mode uses OS font rendering, which produces pixel differences against a headless baseline.

claims.statement: On macOS a visual run launches the browser itself with legacy scroll bars, because Chromium sizes a native select's arrow box from the macOS scroll bar style and overlay scroll bars draw every native select four pixels narrower, which failed a baseline made on a trackpad once a mouse was plugged in.
claims.quote: Visual specs import `test` from `@fixtures/visual`. On macOS it launches Playwright's headless shell with legacy scroll bars (`-AppleShowScrollBars Always`) and connects to it over CDP. Chromium sizes a native `<select>` arrow box from the macOS scroll bar style, and with the default "Show scroll bars: Automatically" setting that style follows whether a mouse is connected: overlay scroll bars on a trackpad alone, legacy ones with a mouse. Overlay scroll bars draw every native select 4px narrower, so a `*-darwin.png` baseline made on a laptop's trackpad failed with a mouse plugged in (704 pixels on the no-JavaScript import reason page), and the other way round. Playwright's own launch refuses an argument that does not start with `-`, so the fixture starts the browser itself. On Linux the fixture is the shared one, unchanged.
claims.note: mechanism: the visual fixture's own browser launch, for the macOS baseline. Names the no-JavaScript import reason page as the page whose baseline differed.

claims.statement: The declaration visual specs set the date of declaration to a fixed string before the screenshot rather than masking it, because the server writes today's date into the page text and a mask is as wide as that text; the date's strong emphasis is proved by the declaration end-to-end specs instead.
claims.quote: The declaration specs set the date of declaration to a fixed string before the screenshot instead of masking it, because the server writes today's date into the page text and a mask is as wide as that text, which changes with the day and month. `freezeDatePickersAt` does not reach that text: it stops the browser clock and moves each date picker's served bounds, and changes nothing the server has already written. The date's strong emphasis is proved by the declaration e2e specs.

claims.statement: Only the animals and plants domains have visual specs.
claims.quote: `animals` and `plants` have `@visual` specs.

claims.statement: Baselines are regenerated by two commands, one for the host-rendered darwin image and one for the container-rendered linux image CI uses, each running every visual spec and writing the updated snapshot into the working tree for commit.
claims.quote:
Regenerate the E2E baseline against the stack frontend with
`npm run test:visual:update:macos` for the host-rendered `*-darwin.png` image and
`npm run test:visual:update:linux` for the container-rendered `*-linux.png` image
used by CI. Both commands run every `@visual` spec and write the
updated snapshot into the working tree for commit.

claims.statement: The Linux baseline script points the service URLs at host.docker.internal and maps localhost to the host, because inside the container localhost is the container.
claims.quote: The Linux script points the service URLs at `host.docker.internal`, because inside the container `localhost` is the container. It also runs the container with `--add-host=localhost:host-gateway`, which maps `localhost` to the host, so any URL the script does not override and that still names `localhost` reaches the stack too.

claims.statement: Every full-page screenshot of a notification page masks the whole status strip, not the reference alone, so the masked box stays a fixed size while the notification reference is minted per run; the strip's own content is covered by an end-to-end spec.
claims.quote:
Every full-page screenshot of a notification page masks the whole status strip. It renders
from the first request and holds the notification reference, which is minted per run. The
whole strip is masked, not the reference alone, so the masked box stays a fixed size. The
strip's own content is covered by `tests/animals/e2e/features/reference-strip.spec.ts`.

claims.statement: A calendar screenshot depends on today's date twice — the browser's today picks the month and highlighted day, and the server's today sets each picker's minimum and maximum date — so the suite stops the browser clock on a fixed day and moves the served bounds by the same number of days.
claims.quote:
A calendar screenshot depends on today's date twice: the browser's today picks the month and
the highlighted day, and the server's today sets each picker's `data-min-date` and
`data-max-date`. `freezeDatePickersAt` (`utils/frozen-date-picker.ts`) stops the browser clock
on a fixed day and moves the served bounds by the same number of days, so the calendar looks
as it would if that day were today.

claims.statement: The security scan is a dynamic application security test using OWASP ZAP as a proxy, with Playwright driving real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl, so it observes what a real session touches and then attacks that.
claims.quote: A DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scan using [OWASP ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/) as a proxy. Playwright drives real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl, so it observes what a real session touches and then attacks that.

claims.statement: Security coverage is traffic-driven, so a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan, which is why the active corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.
claims.quote: Coverage is therefore **traffic-driven**: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan. That is why the `@active` corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.

claims.statement: There are two security profiles: a passive scan across the end-to-end suite excluding the active corpus, cheap enough to run broadly, and a passive plus scoped active scan against the active suite alone, which attacks and runs on docker-compose only.
claims.quote:
| `security`        | The e2e suite, excluding `@active` | No — passive only | Cheap, run broadly              |
| `security:active` | The `@active` suite only           | Yes               | Deliberate; docker-compose only |

claims.statement: The active suite is excluded from the passive profile because it walks the same journeys a second time and includes destructive steps.
claims.quote: `@active` is excluded from the passive profile because it walks the same journeys a second time and includes destructive steps.

claims.statement: The scan runs in three lanes: locally against the localhost stack on both profiles and per domain except plants, as a GitHub Action against a stack on the runner for the full active corpus, and from the CDP Portal against the deployed environment for the passive profile only.
claims.quote: | **Local**         | `npm run test:docker-compose[:<domain>]:security`, `npm run test:docker-compose[:<domain>]:security:active` | `playwright.docker-compose.config.ts` | localhost stack           | both; each also per domain (not plants) |

claims.statement: The active profile is refused on CDP because the active suite deletes notifications, documents and dead-letter messages and the scan re-fires each with fuzzed payloads, which is fine against a disposable stack and destructive against a shared one; the production guard is no help because it stops prod alone, so dev, test and perf-test would all have run.
claims.quote: **`security:active` is refused on CDP.** The `@active` suite deletes notifications, documents and DLQ messages, and the active scan re-fires each with fuzzed payloads — fine against a disposable stack, destructive against a shared one. `entrypoint.sh` writes to `FAILED` rather than running it. The `throwIfProdEnvironment` guard is no help here: it stops `prod` alone, so `dev`, `test` and `perf-test` would all have run.

claims.statement: The security GitHub Action's report publishes to GitHub Pages under a dated security-active path, password-protected because that Pages site is otherwise public, and reports older than seven days are pruned.
claims.quote: The GitHub Action is manual dispatch only; the nightly schedule stays disabled pending a verified end-to-end run. Its report publishes to GitHub Pages under `security-active/<date>/`, password-protected via the `ZAP_REPORT_PASSWORD` secret because that Pages site is otherwise public. Reports older than 7 days are pruned.

claims.statement: The scheduled security scan workflow runs at 01:00 UTC on weekdays as well as on manual dispatch, and calls the workspace's active-scan workflow.
claims.quote:
on:
  schedule:
    # 01:00 UTC, weekdays only.
    - cron: '0 1 * * 1-5'
  workflow_dispatch:
claims.note: Ambiguity recorded, not resolved: docs/security.md:28 and README.md:524 both say the scan is manual dispatch only and the schedule stays disabled, while the workflow file carries an enabled weekday cron.

claims.statement: A local security run needs the app stack up and ZAP brought up additively on the stack's security profile, which waits for health checks so it returns only once ZAP is accepting requests.
claims.quote: 2. Bring up ZAP too — additive, and waits for healthchecks so it returns only once ZAP is accepting requests: `tim docker up --profile security`

claims.statement: The full active scan is the authoritative clean bill of health, and a per-domain active run is marked as scoped in its report.
claims.quote: Full `security:active` is the authoritative clean bill of health. Per-domain active sets `ZAP_SCOPE` so the no-traffic gate only covers that domain's contexts; the report is labelled as scoped.

claims.statement: Each run clears the ZAP report directory first, so running two domains back to back keeps only the second domain's report.
claims.quote: Each run clears `zap-report/` first, so running two domains back to back keeps only the second domain's report.

claims.statement: ZAP needs host networking on Docker Desktop for Mac to resolve the stack's localhost OIDC redirects, which OrbStack supports out of the box and Docker Desktop needs 4.34 or later with host networking enabled.
claims.quote: > **Docker Desktop for Mac:** ZAP needs `network_mode: host` to resolve the stack's `localhost` OIDC redirects. OrbStack supports this out of the box; Docker Desktop needs 4.34+ with host networking enabled in Settings (off by default).

claims.statement: ZAP runs as part of the shared workspace stack locally and as an in-process daemon on CDP, reusing the same plan files and gate.
claims.quote: ZAP runs as part of the shared workspace stack (`docker/stack/security.compose.yml`). On CDP the same plan files and gate are reused, with ZAP as an in-process daemon rather than a container.

claims.quote:
| `trade-imports-animals-frontend` | 3000       | `frontend`        |

claims.statement: The active corpus is written against the three frontends, and the three APIs are scanned all the same because every API client is built from Playwright's own request fixture, which inherits the project's proxy, so seeding and assertion calls reach ZAP as real traffic.
claims.quote: The `@active` corpus is written against the three frontends. The three APIs are scanned all the same: every API client here is built from Playwright's own `request` fixture, which inherits the project's proxy, so the specs' seeding and assertion calls reach ZAP as real traffic.

claims.statement: Diagnostics are excluded from the scan rather than scanned: health and static assets on the Node contexts, and the full actuator set of health, info, metrics, cache and env on the three Java services.
claims.quote: Ports are the compose stack's; on CDP each service is a per-service subdomain. Diagnostics are excluded rather than scanned: `/health` and static assets on the Node contexts, and the full actuator set (`/health`, `/info`, `/metrics`, `/cache`, `/env`) on the three Java services.

claims.statement: The Defra ID stub is observed passively and never attacked because it is a temporary sign-in stub the team does not own, while the service's own sign-in and sign-in-oidc handlers are in scope since the OIDC callback and its redirect parameter outlive the stub.
claims.quote: | `trade-imports-defra-id-stub` (3007) | A temporary sign-in stub we do not own. Observed passively, never attacked. Our own `/auth/sign-in` and `/auth/sign-in-oidc` handlers **are** in scope — the OIDC callback and its `redirect` parameter outlive the stub. |

claims.statement: The CDP uploader is not scanned because the browser posts uploads to the frontend, which forwards them server-side, so the uploader never enters the site tree.
claims.quote: | `cdp-uploader` (7337)                | A platform component. The browser posts uploads to the frontend, which forwards them server-side, so the uploader never enters the site tree.                                                                             |

claims.quote: | `trade-imports-ins-backend` (8090)   | An SQS consumer with no HTTP controllers. Its risk boundary is the queue, which DAST cannot reach; the API that produces those events is scanned.                                                                         |

claims.statement: One INS active spec drives the sign-in round trip and holds the only check that the INS front door renders a sign-out link, every other spec starting pre-authenticated.
claims.quote: - **Sign-in round trip.** `/auth/sign-in` and `/auth/sign-in-oidc` are in scope, and every other spec starts pre-authenticated, so `address-book-auth.spec.ts` is the only spec that drives them. It also holds the only check that INS renders a sign-out link: if the sign-out step fails, check that first before assuming the route moved.

claims.statement: The INS active address-book spec adds one address through the add route and views, edits and deletes it through the per-address route, and opens a tab filtered by a role so the scan reaches the list's address-type and role parameters.
claims.quote: - **Record lifecycle.** `address-book.spec.ts` adds one address through `/address-book/add`, and views, edits and deletes it through `/address-book/{addressId}`; the `addressId` dataDrivenNode has nothing to fold without them. It also opens a tab and filters it by a role, so the scan reaches the list's `addressType` and `role` parameters.

claims.statement: The INS active address-book spec also opens the add page with the four handshake query parameters journey-type, notification-id, fulfilment-id and handshake-token, which no other spec sends, and only the rejected-guard path is provable there because no accepted token can be seeded.
claims.quote: - **Handshake query parameters.** `address-book.spec.ts` also opens the add page with `journey-type`, `notification-id`, `fulfilment-id` and `handshake-token`, which no other spec sends. Only the rejected-guard path is provable here; extend it to a real accepted token if seeding one becomes possible.

claims.statement: A security run fails on a FAIL-rated alert, where a rules file maps ZAP plugin ids to ignore, warn or fail and anything unlisted defaults to fail if it is High risk and warn otherwise.
claims.quote: - **A FAIL-rated alert.** `zap/rules.tsv` maps ZAP plugin ids to `IGNORE`/`WARN`/`FAIL`; anything unlisted defaults to FAIL if High risk and WARN otherwise.

claims.statement: A security run fails on a truncated scan: each context is capped at 60 minutes, the cap setting must match that number exactly, and a scan that finishes at the ceiling was cut short, an incomplete scan reporting no findings being a false clean.
claims.quote: - **A truncated scan.** Each context is capped at 60 minutes (`maxScanDurationInMins`), and `ACTIVE_SCAN_CAP_MINS` must match that number exactly. A scan that finishes at the ceiling was cut short, and an incomplete scan reporting no findings is a false clean.

claims.statement: A security run fails on a declared context that saw no traffic, because its active-scan job scanned nothing and reported clean; this gate applies to the active profile only and a scoped run gates only that domain's contexts.
claims.quote: - **A context with no traffic.** Declared but undriven means its activeScan job scanned nothing and reported clean. Active profile only. Per-domain active (`ZAP_SCOPE`) gates only that domain's contexts; the report callout marks the run as scoped.

claims.statement: ZAP is enabled only when the profile is exactly security or security:active, and anything other than an exact active value is treated as passive rather than the reverse.
claims.quote: export const zapEnabled = process.env.PROFILE === 'security' || process.env.PROFILE === 'security:active';

claims.statement: ZAP listens on port 9095 by default, deliberately outside the workspace's growing 3xxx Node and 808x Java port sequences.
claims.quote: export const zapPort = process.env.ZAP_PORT || '9095';
claims.note: The file's comment gives the reason: a workspace-assigned range only grows, so the next free slot today is taken by the next new service eventually. The default local API key is a development placeholder and is not quoted here.

claims.statement: A passive run uses one automation plan file and an active run another, and a separate context plan registers the contexts before any traffic exists so new site-tree nodes are classified correctly as the Playwright run creates them.
The ZAP plan directory differs by lane: locally ZAP runs in its own container with the plan files bind-mounted, while on CDP the same-container sidecar reads them from the checked-out repo.
claims.quote: const zapPlanDir = process.env.ZAP_PLAN_DIR || '/zap/plan';

claims.statement: A CDP Portal run chooses its suite with a PROFILE value, and an unset PROFILE runs the default profile.
claims.quote:
In the CDP Portal, provide a `PROFILE` value to choose which test suite the container runs via `entrypoint.sh`.
If `PROFILE` is not set, the `default` profile is used.

claims.statement: A CDP profile can be scoped to one domain by prefixing the suite with the domain name, for any of e2e, a11y, dynamics, cross-browser, browserstack, security and the refused active security, where the domain is animals, animals-admin, ins or plants.
claims.quote:
The profiles above run every domain. To run one domain's suite only, prefix the
suite with its domain name as `<domain>:<suite>`:

claims.statement: A domain-scoped profile for a test type the domain has no specs of, such as accessibility for plants today, fails with Playwright's no tests found.
claims.quote:
`<domain>` is one of `animals`, `animals-admin`, `ins` or `plants`, e.g.
